issues.legal_issue: An assembly formed to defend property against theft by force within the lawful limits of private defence is not an unlawful assembly merely because it seeks to enforce a right.
material_facts: The High Court found that the respondents’ group was in possession of the land and that members of the prosecution party were stealing fruit from it.
The group’s object was to prevent the theft in exercise of the right of private defence of property.

The High Court found that the right of private defence extended to causing death in the circumstances, subject to legal restrictions, but that the person or persons who caused the deaths exceeded that right.
issues.conclusion: The group’s object of preventing the theft in exercise of the right of private defence was not unlawful, so the respondents could not be treated as members of an unlawful assembly on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 141, including its fourth clause, must be read with sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code. Under section 96, an act done in the exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence; asserting that right within its lawful limits is not enforcing a right by criminal force for the purposes of section 141. The Court relied on Kapildeo Singh v. The King and Kishori Prasad v. State of Bihar, which support the principle that an assembly defending property by force within the limits prescribed by law is not thereby an unlawful assembly.

predicates.assembly_of_five_or_more: Five or more persons assembled together.
predicates.common_object_is_to_defend_property_from: The assembled persons shared the object of preventing theft of property they possessed.
predicates.force_used_for_that_object_is_within_law: The force used to prevent the theft was within the lawful limits of private defence.

issues.definition: When five or more persons share an object of defending possessed property from theft and use force within lawful defence limits, their object is not unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an assembly are not constructively liable for murder when the assembly’s common object is lawful defence of property and the killings are neither in prosecution of that object nor known to be likely in its prosecution.
material_facts: The group’s common object was to prevent theft of fruit from land it possessed, not to kill the two victims.
The persons who caused the deaths exceeded the right of private defence.
The evidence did not establish which respondents were armed with the weapons that caused the fatal wounds or who inflicted those wounds.
The deaths were not committed in prosecution of the group’s common object, and the members were not shown to know that the deaths were likely to be committed in prosecution of that object.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could not be convicted of murder through constructive liability based on membership of the assembly; any person who exceeded the right of private defence could be individually responsible if the evidence established that person’s responsibility.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof of an unlawful assembly and that the offence was committed in prosecution of its common object, or was one the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Read with sections 96 to 106, a lawful object of private defence does not establish an unlawful assembly merely because individuals exceed that defence. The Court relied on Kapildeo Singh v. The King and Kishori Prasad v. State of Bihar. It distinguished Gurudittamal v. State of U.P., where the individual appellants’ killings and their common intention had been established.

rule.if: constructive_homicide_case and common_object_is_to_defend_property_from_theft and killers_exceeded_defence_limits and not murder_was_in_prosecution_of_common_object and not members_knew_murder_was_likely_in_prosecution_of_common_object

predicates.constructive_homicide_case: The prosecution seeks to hold people liable for a homicide committed by a member of an assembly because of their membership of that assembly.
predicates.common_object_is_to_defend_property_from: The assembly’s shared object was to prevent theft of property it possessed.
predicates.killers_exceeded_defence_limits: The person or persons who caused the deaths used force exceeding the lawful limits of defence.
predicates.murder_was_in_prosecution_of_common_obje: The murder was committed to advance the assembly’s common object.
predicates.members_knew_murder_was_likely_in_prosec: The assembly members knew that murder was likely to be committed in advancing the common object.

issues.definition: Assembly members are not constructively liable for murder when the group sought to defend property from theft, the killers exceeded lawful defence, and the murder was neither in prosecution of nor known to be likely in prosecution of the group’s object.

issues.legal_issue: Joint murder liability based on common intention cannot be imposed when a shared intention to murder has not been established.
material_facts: The respondents wanted to prevent the collection of fruit from land in their possession.
A common intention among the respondents to murder either victim was not established.
The evidence did not establish which respondents caused the fatal wounds.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could not be convicted of murder on the basis of common intention.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires a common intention to commit the offence for joint liability. The Court relied on Kishori Prasad v. State of Bihar and distinguished Gurudittamal v. State of U.P., where a common intention to kill had been found.

predicates.joint_homicide_liability_case: The prosecution seeks to hold multiple people jointly liable for murder based on their shared intention.
predicates.shared_intention_to_murder: The people charged shared an intention to kill the victim or victims.

issues.definition: When a prosecution seeks joint murder liability but a shared intention to murder is not established, that basis for joint liability does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Factual findings supporting an acquittal should not be disturbed in an appeal when they are supported by adequate evidence and are not perverse.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the High Court’s acquittal and its findings concerning possession of the land, theft of the fruit, and the right of private defence.
The Supreme Court found that those findings were based on adequate evidence and were not shown to be perverse.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with those findings in the appeal against acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: In the appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution from an acquittal, the Court declined to disturb factual findings that were supported by adequate evidence and were not shown to be perverse.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and findings_supported_by_adequate_evidence and not findings_are_perverse

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The case is an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.findings_supported_by_adequate_evidence: The challenged factual findings are supported by adequate evidence.
predicates.findings_are_perverse: The challenged factual findings are perverse.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, factual findings supported by adequate evidence and not perverse are not disturbed.
